summary: Queen's Wharf Lighthouse: an 1861 wooden range tower for Toronto Harbour, out of service after the 1911 season, moved to Fleet Street in 1929 and now owned by the City of Toronto.

structures.note: Rear (Red) range light of the 1861 pair; moved about 450 m in 1929

White front light; destroyed by fire on 1 September (Lighthouse Friends: 1918; the Department's report for the Harbour Commission year ending 31 December 1917: 1917). The Department's 1919 volume says built 1856.

access.note: On Fleet Street, Toronto. Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Owned by the City of Toronto.

events.note: Square wooden tower about 16 ft (5 m) placed on Queen's Wharf as a guide for vessels entering the harbour
Pair of range lights built to Kivas Tully's design; tenders advertised May and June 1861; keeper's dwelling built with them
Front (white) light moved to the north-west corner of the wharf: about 30 ft (Lighthouse Friends quoting the Commissioners) or 40 ft (Department's 1902 report)
Steamer Resolute, of Desoronto, foundered outside the western entrance on 22 November 1906 (Department) or 21 November (Lighthouse Friends)
Fire at Queen's Wharf on 8 July 1908 consumed the boat house; the lighthouses and dwelling were saved, with some injury

Lighthouse Friends and the marker: range lights discontinued at the end of the 1911 season. The Department's reports record the Queen's Wharf lamps lit 28 March 1910 (discontinued 8 December 1910) and 30 March 1911 (discontinued 8 December 1911). No report read gives a 1912 lighting.
Storm signals displayed at Queen's Wharf and Eastern Gap during the 1912 season; the Department counts sixteen occasions

Abandoned front (white) range light destroyed by fire on 1 September: Lighthouse Friends gives 1918; the Department's report for the Harbour Commission year ending 31 December 1917 gives 1917. See resolved_conflicts.
Toronto Harbour Commission transferred the remaining tower to the City of Toronto
Moved about 450 m on wooden rollers to Fleet Street later in 1929 (Lighthouse Friends says west; the ACO record says north)
City of Toronto restored the building

corrections.why: Lighthouse Friends, the marker and the ACO record all name the City of Toronto as owner. The TTC's streetcar loop surrounds the tower; the sources read here do not say the TTC runs the lighthouse.

The sources read here date the tower to the 1861 pair (Lighthouse Friends; ACO) and say it was moved in 1929. No source read here gives 1931 for the tower; the 1931 date may belong to the adjacent streetcar loop. The 'built 1931' event should also come out.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1838 first lit is the square wooden guide tower placed on the wharf (Lighthouse Friends). Wikidata's 1861 is the Tully pair that survives. Both dates belong to the site; the 1838 tower is not the surviving building.

Settled as far as the sources go. Lighthouse Friends and the marker say the range lights were discontinued in 1911. The Department's reports record the lamps lit 28 March 1910 and discontinued 8 December 1910, and lit 30 March 1911 and discontinued 8 December 1911. They agree with the 1911 end date. No source read gives a 1912 lighting.

Lighthouse Friends gives 1 September 1918 for the fire that destroyed the abandoned front light. The Department's report includes the Toronto Harbour Commission account for the year ending 31 December 1917, which gives 1 September with the year 1917. Left for a human reader.

notes_for_editor: Rich station, but almost all the narrative comes from Lighthouse Friends (facts only, one short quote per page) and the Department's annual reports. The keeper list and the 1901, 1908 and 1911 Commissioners' details are Lighthouse Friends quoting the Toronto Harbour Commissioners' annual reports, which are NOT in our corpus; those are cited to Lighthouse Friends and have not been checked against the originals. Newspapers: none searched. Toronto papers (the Globe, Toronto Star, Toronto Sun) are not in Chronicling America, and the Wikipedia article's Globe citations were not read as sources (Wikipedia is a lead only). CONFLICTS LEFT IN THE TEXT: (1) pier 1830 (LF) vs 1833 (ACO); (2) front light moved 30 ft (LF quoting Commissioners) vs 40 ft (DMF 1902) in 1901; (3) front light 'built in 1856' (DMF 1919) vs 1861 (LF, ACO, marker); (4) 1929 move west (LF) vs north (ACO); (5) Resolute: 21 Nov (LF) vs 22 Nov (DMF), 'five occupants of a lifeboat' (LF) vs six drowned (DMF), coal and schooner in LF only; (6) no conflict on the 1911 end: LF and the marker say 1911, and the Department's Harbour Commission reports record the lamps lit 30 March and discontinued 8 December 1911 (the 1913 volume's lamp line is the 1911 season, not 1912); the 1912 lighting in the earlier draft was a misdate. (7) fire on the abandoned front light: 1 September 1918 (LF) vs 1 September 1917 (Department's report reprinting the Harbour Commission account for the year ending 31 December 1917). RECORD CORRECTIONS: agency TTC (owner is the City; TTC operates the Fleet loop per Wikipedia, which is not cited) and '1931 built' (the Fleet Loop opened 1931 per Wikipedia; not sourced here). The record's 'light.deactivated 1912' is not supported by any report read; the Department's reports give the 1911 season as the last lit (discontinued 8 December 1911). MATCHED BY POSITION: none. The 1901 Chief Engineer's 'moved 40 feet' line is on scan 67, printed p. 51, of 1902v36i9p21_0083 (the corpus index gave scan 66). Fact-checker, 2026-10-28: all seven annual-report citations (fn4 to fn10) were one scan low in the corpus index; each was checked against the PDF page and its printed number. Three date errors were corrected: the 1910 and 1911 lamp seasons (not 1911 and 1912), and the fire year (1917 in the year-ending-31-Dec-1917 account, against LF's 1918). Other Wikipedia facts not used here: the 1885 move of the red light (cited to the Globe), the 1973 heritage register listing and the Fleet Loop lease. Photos: none added; ACO and Toronto Public Library images may be usable later, but licences were not checked.
